subject: Climate & Environment
title: Ice Sheet Collapse
description: Learn Ice Sheet Collapse in one minute.

hook.text: Antarctica's Thwaites Glacier is called the Doomsday Glacier. It earned that name.

buildup.text: Warm ocean water melts it from underneath, loosening its grip on the bedrock below.

discovery.text: If Thwaites collapses, it could raise sea levels by 65 centimeters on its own.

twist.text: It also acts as a cork. Its loss would let neighboring glaciers slide into the sea.

climax.text: Total potential sea rise from West Antarctica alone is over 3 meters.

punchline.text: One glacier holds back a flood that could reshape every coast.

quiz.question: Why is Thwaites Glacier called the Doomsday Glacier?
options: Its collapse would trigger massive sea level rise
It's the coldest place on Earth

details.summary: Ice-sheet collapse refers to the rapid, potentially irreversible breakup of major ice masses when warming crosses critical thresholds. West Antarctica's Thwaites Glacier, dubbed the Doomsday Glacier, could trigger over 3 meters of eventual sea-level rise if it destabilizes.
details.whyItMatters: Collapse events are among the most feared climate tipping points because they are essentially irreversible on human timescales and would reshape global coastlines.
takeaways: Thwaites Glacier alone could contribute over 60 cm of sea-level rise
Its destabilization could unlock wider West Antarctic collapse
Warm ocean water undermining the glacier is the primary risk

faq.question: Why is Thwaites called the Doomsday Glacier?
faq.answer: Thwaites Glacier is the size of Great Britain and acts as a cork holding back the broader West Antarctic Ice Sheet. If it collapses, it could trigger a chain reaction releasing over 3 meters of sea-level rise over centuries.

faq.question: How soon could ice-sheet collapse happen?
faq.answer: Thwaites is already retreating at an accelerating rate. Some researchers suggest significant destabilization could begin within decades, though complete collapse would unfold over centuries. The timeline remains one of climate science's biggest uncertainties.
